thesis.title: Graded Predictivism: Measuring Accommodation in Bits of Leakage
thesis.thesis: How far a fit's confirmatory force should be discounted for accommodation is bounded by the mutual information between the data and the choice of hypothesis. 'Prediction' is the special case where that information is zero. Timing matters only as a crude upper bound on this leakage.
thesis.argument_sketch: Results in adaptive data analysis (Russo and Zou; Dwork et al.) bound the bias of a data-selected statistic by I(E; choice of H). I adapt these bounds to the evidential setting and show that the excess apparent support of a selected hypothesis over its honest support is controlled by this quantity. The prediction/accommodation dichotomy therefore conceals a continuum. Examples on the continuum include hypotheses chosen after seeing a noisy summary of the data, a coarse histogram, or one variable among many, and each warrants intermediate confirmation. Timing is neither necessary nor sufficient for zero leakage: post-data choices made blind to the data have none, and pre-data choices informed by correlated pilot data have some.
thesis.why_new: The philosophical literature treats novelty as binary, whether temporal (Popper, Lakatos), heuristic (Zahar, Worrall), or use-based. The information-theoretic results in computer science have not been brought into confirmation theory. This thesis supplies a quantitative, graded replacement for use-novelty and makes Worrall's criterion a limiting case.

objection.objection: The argument moves from a property of selection procedures to a claim about the confirmation of a particular hypothesis, and that move does not go through. The Russo–Zou and Dwork et al. bounds have the form |E[φ_T − μ_T]| ≤ σ√(2 I(T; data)). This is a bound on expected bias, averaged over the joint distribution of datasets and the choices a fixed selection rule would make on them. I(E; choice of H) is therefore not a feature of the actual episode, in which this E was observed and this H was proposed. It is a feature of a counterfactual policy: what the scientist would have chosen had the data come out otherwise. Confirmation, on any standard account (Bayesian, likelihoodist, or Hempelian), is a relation between the actual E and the actual H. Three problems follow. (i) Indeterminacy: a scientist who looks at the data and proposes H usually has no well-defined selection rule over alternative datasets. The value of I depends on how that counterfactual policy is specified, so the advertised continuum inherits a reference-class problem. Your own examples (blind post-data choice, pilot-informed pre-data choice) get their verdicts only because the procedure is stipulated, not because anything about the evidence fixes it. (ii) Expectation versus single case: a small average I is compatible with large realized leakage in the actual case (high pointwise mutual information on this dataset), and a large I is compatible with negligible leakage here. A bound on expected bias therefore cannot bound the discount owed to the fit actually in hand. To get a single-case bound you would need high-probability or pointwise results, such as the max-information bounds in Dwork et al. 2015, 'Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse'. Those bounds are not mutual-information bounds, so the thesis as stated would not survive the substitution. (iii) The quantity being bounded is not confirmation. The 'excess apparent support' that selection inflates is excess only relative to an unconditioned, frequentist measure of fit. Under a Bayesian treatment, data-dependent selection of which hypothesis to report is ignorable whenever the prior over hypotheses is fixed in advance and the selection depends only on the data (Dawid 1994, 'Selection paradoxes of Bayesian inference'). The posterior for the selected H is then exactly as it should be, and nothing needs discounting. So either the thesis assumes procedure-relative confirmation, which begs the question against the likelihood principle (Royall 1997; Howson & Urbach) and needs defending, or it is a thesis about error rates of procedures. In the second case it is a refinement of Mayo's severity framework, not a result about confirmation. Neither option delivers the advertised claim that the prediction/accommodation distinction in confirmation theory conceals an information-theoretic continuum.
objection.rationale: This objection targets the bridge principle the whole paper rests on: that a bound on the expected bias of a data-selected statistic is a bound on how much the confirmatory force of a particular fit should be discounted. If the objection goes unanswered, the formal results stay true but say nothing about confirmation. They become results about the reliability of policies, and the dissolution of the prediction/accommodation debate (White 2003; Lipton; Hitchcock & Sober 2004) does not follow. The claims about timing also lose their force, because they rely on I being determinate for actual cases. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because the author has a recoverable position. They can openly adopt an error-statistical or procedure-relative conception of support, argue that confirmation of a reported hypothesis is properly relative to the process that generated the report, and replace the mutual-information bounds with max-information or pointwise bounds that apply to single cases. That is a substantial rewrite with a narrower conclusion, but it is not an abandonment of the project.

closest_work.work: Russo, D. & Zou, J. (2016, AISTATS; expanded 2020, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory), 'Controlling Bias in Adaptive Data Analysis Using Information Theory' / 'How much does your data exploration overfit?'

Its examples already include noisy selection, coarsened selection, and selection among many variables. The thesis's 'continuum' examples are largely Russo and Zou's examples relabelled. What remains new is the translation from 'bias of an estimate' to 'excess confirmation', and that translation is the step that needs defending.

closest_work.work: Fithian, Sun & Taylor (2014), 'Optimal Inference After Model Selection'; Tian & Taylor (2018, Ann. Stat.), 'Selective inference with a randomized response'
closest_work.relation: This is selective inference with randomization ('data carving'). This is the 'noisy summary' point on the continuum, already formalized exactly, with no bound needed.

closest_work.work: Hitchcock, C. & Sober, E. (2004, BJPS), 'Prediction Versus Accommodation and the Risk of Overfitting'
closest_work.relation: This is the closest philosophical precedent. It argues that any epistemic advantage of prediction is contingent and stems from the overfitting risk of accommodation, tied to model-selection criteria (AIC). The thesis is in effect an information-theoretic sharpening of Hitchcock and Sober. It should be framed as such, not as overturning a dichotomy.

closest_work.work: Zahar (1973); Worrall (1978, 1989, 2014 'Prediction and accommodation revisited'); Gardner (1982, BJPS), 'Predicting Novel Facts'
closest_work.relation: The claim that timing is neither necessary nor sufficient, and that what matters is whether the data were used in constructing the hypothesis ('use-novelty', 'heuristic novelty'), is standard. It dates to the 1970s and 80s. The pilot-data point is a modest addition.

closest_work.work: Mayo, D. (1996, Error and the Growth of Experimental Knowledge, ch. 8; 2008 with Cox; 2018, Statistical Inference as Severe Testing)
closest_work.relation: Mayo argues that use-novelty is a crude proxy, and that what matters is whether the use of data in constructing H damages the error probabilities (severity) of the test. This is the same structural thesis as yours ('timing/use is a proxy for something else'), with severity in place of mutual information.

closest_work.work: White, R. (2003, Mind), 'The Epistemic Advantage of Prediction over Accommodation'; Lange, M. (2001, Phil Sci), 'The Apparent Superiority of Prediction to Accommodation as a Side Effect'; Barnes, E. C. (2008), The Paradox of Predictivism; Douglas & Magnus (2013, SHPS)
closest_work.relation: These are graded or 'weak' predictivisms on which prediction's advantage is a proxy for some further variable: reliability of the hypothesis-generating process, coincidence-avoidance, or the predictor's credibility. White's 'reliability of the selection mechanism' is close in spirit to treating the selection channel as the relevant variable.

novelty.note: Verdict 'partly'. The mathematics is wholly borrowed, and the continuum with noisy or coarse selection is already explicit in Russo & Zou and in randomized selective inference. The 'timing is a proxy' thesis is decades old (Worrall, Gardner, Mayo, Hitchcock & Sober). I am not aware of a published philosophy paper that explicitly states predictivism as an MI bound on selection leakage, so the bridge itself may be new. I cannot run a literature search here, so check PhilPapers and recent BJPS/Phil Sci/Synthese issues before claiming priority. Whatever novelty there is rests on the bridge, and the bridge has four substantive problems as sketched. (1) Wrong quantity. Russo-Zou bound expected bias of a subgaussian statistic. 'Confirmatory force' of a particular selected H on a particular data set is not an expectation over selection runs. You need an argument that the relevant discount is the average over the selection channel and not conditional on the realized choice. Max-information (Dwork et al.; Rogers et al.) gives high-probability control and is the better-motivated measure for single-case warrant. MI can be small while a rare, highly informative selection event occurs. (2) 'Bounded by' is not 'measured by'. The MI result gives an upper bound, so zero MI implies no bias, but positive MI does not imply a discount of that size, or any discount. The thesis title claims the bound. The argument as sketched supports only sufficiency of zero leakage. (3) The Bayesian objection is not addressed. A Bayesian who conditions on the total evidence, including the fact and mechanism of selection, needs no discount (Howson & Urbach; Kahn, Landsberg & Stockman 1992). 'Excess apparent support' then measures only an agent's failure to condition properly, and MI quantifies how much such a mistake can cost. That is a claim about heuristics, not about confirmation. You must say which. (4) 'Prediction is the special case where information is zero' is false as stated. Theories proposed before the data are typically built on correlated earlier data and background theory, so I(E; choice of H) > 0 for most genuine predictions. Your own pilot-data example concedes this. The framework therefore dissolves the prediction category rather than reconstructing it. That may be the right conclusion, but it should be the stated one.

# Leakage, Not Timing: An Information-Theoretic Account of the Accommodation Discount

## 1. Introduction

Predictivism holds that evidence a hypothesis predicted supports it more than evidence it was built to accommodate. The view has been defended on Bayesian grounds (Maher 1988; Lipton 2004; White 2003; Hitchcock and Sober 2004; Barnes 2008), restricted on error-statistical grounds (Mayo 1996, 2018), and rejected by those who take confirmation to be a timeless relation between evidence and hypothesis (Howson and Urbach 2006). I defend the following thesis. How far a fit's confirmatory force should be discounted for accommodation is controlled by the information that flowed from the data into the choice of hypothesis. "Prediction" is the case where that flow is zero. Timing matters only because it is a coarse indicator of whether any flow occurred.

My motivation came from adaptive data analysis. Russo and Zou (2016, 2020) showed that if a statistic $\phi_t(X)$ is $\sigma$-subgaussian for each fixed $t$, and a hypothesis $T$ is selected using the data $X$, then

$$\big|\mathbb{E}[\phi_T(X)-\mu_T]\big| \le \sigma\sqrt{2\,I(T;X)}.$$

Related results by Dwork et al. (2015a, 2015b, 2015c) bound selection bias by quantities such as max-information and differential privacy. The tempting philosophical gloss is that accommodation inflates apparent support in proportion to information leakage.

A referee raised a three-part objection to this gloss, and I think it is correct as aimed at it. First, $I(T;X)$ is a property of a selection *policy*, which is a counterfactual and often indeterminate thing. Confirmation, by contrast, relates the actual $E$ to the actual $H$. Second, an expected-bias bound cannot bound the discount owed in the single case. Third, the quantity being bounded is a frequentist excess of fit, not confirmation. Dawid (1994) showed that for a Bayesian with a fixed prior, data-dependent selection is ignorable. So the thesis either begs the question against the likelihood principle or collapses into a refinement of severity.

This essay restates the thesis so that it survives these points. The restatement makes four changes.

1. **Relocation.** The discount does not attach to the evidential import of the data. It attaches to the evidential import of a second observation: *that this hypothesis was proposed*. On this reading, the account is ordinary total-evidence Bayesianism and complies with the likelihood principle.
2. **Conditioning.** The relevant information is $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$, leakage *given the world*, not $I(T;X)$. The unconditional quantity would wrongly count a reliable theorist's correct prediction as leakage.
3. **Two levels.** In the single case the discount is given *exactly* by pointwise information densities. Their mean, the mutual information, bounds the expected discount. Their supremum, a two-sided max-information, bounds the single case uniformly.
4. **Channels, not policies.** The bounds depend only on the information channel through which the data reached the proposer, which is fixed by the causal history of the episode. They do not depend on the proposer's indeterminate dispositions.

With these changes the original claim survives. The prediction/accommodation dichotomy conceals a continuum, and the continuum lives in confirmation theory proper, not merely in the theory of error rates. Section 2 sets up the framework and proves two simple results. Section 3 defends the conditioning. Sections 4–6 answer the objection's three parts, in the order (iii), (ii), (i), because the answer to (iii) supplies the machinery for the other two. Section 7 locates timing on the continuum. Section 8 states limits.

## 2. The proposal as evidence

### 2.1 The setup

Let $\Theta$ range over candidate states of the world. For simplicity, identify each state with a hypothesis in a countable space $\mathcal{H}$; nothing turns on this. Let $X$ be the data, and let $T\in\mathcal{H}$ be the hypothesis a scientist puts forward as the one to be assessed. The joint distribution is

$$p(\theta,x,t)=p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta).$$

The factor $p(t\mid x,\theta)$ models the proposer. It can depend on $\theta$ in two ways. One route runs through $x$. The other runs through whatever else the proposer has access to that bears on $\theta$: theoretical insight, background knowledge, analogies, other experiments. Write $Z$ for that other access, and assume for now that it is conditionally independent of $X$ given $\Theta$.

An evaluator who learns that $t$ was proposed and that the data are $x$ has total evidence $(x,t)$. The correct posterior is

$$p(\theta\mid x,t)\ \propto\ p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta).$$

This already contains the key point. The proposal event is an observation with its own likelihood. Whether it is evidentially relevant, and how much, depends on how $p(t\mid x,\theta)$ varies with $\theta$ at the actual $(x,t)$.

### 2.2 Prediction and the predictivist evaluator

Call a proposal *predictive*, in the structural sense, iff $T\perp X\mid \Theta$. In that case $p(t\mid x,\theta)=p(t\mid\theta)$ and the likelihood factors:

$$p(\theta\mid x,t)\ \propto\ p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid\theta).$$

The proposal now contributes the ratio $p(t\mid\theta)/p(t\mid\theta')$. This is the proposer's reliability: how much more often this proposer would put $t$ forward if $\theta$ held than if $\theta'$ did. It is the quantity that the Bayesian defences of predictivism exploit. White (2003) argues that a successful prediction is evidence that the theorist was reliably tracking the truth. Maher (1988) argues that it is evidence about the method that produced the hypothesis. Lipton (2004) argues that accommodation raises the suspicion of a "fudged" theory. In each case, the premium for prediction is the evidential weight of the proposal.

Now define the **predictivist evaluator** $q$. This evaluator applies the factored likelihood whatever the proposal's actual provenance:

$$q(\theta,x,t)=p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid\theta),$$

where $p(t\mid\theta)=\sum_x p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta)$ is the proposer's true marginal reliability. This evaluator does the natural thing with a track record. They know how often this proposer's hypotheses are true, they see that the data fit, and they multiply. For predictions, $q=p$ and the computation is exact.

I define the **accommodation discount** as the difference between the $q$-posterior and the $p$-posterior. It is the excess apparent support that a hypothesis receives when its proposal is credited as independent evidence even though it was not independent of the data. This is the explicandum of the thesis.

One consequence is worth stating immediately. If the proposer's choice depends on $\theta$ *only* through $x$, so that $p(t\mid x,\theta)=p(t\mid x)$, then that factor is constant in $\theta$ and cancels. The correct posterior is just $p(\theta\mid x)$, and the proposal adds nothing. This is Dawid's (1994) ignorability result, seen from inside the framework. Section 4 returns to it. Here I note only that Dawid's case is not a counterexample to the discount. It is the case of *maximal* discount: the predictivist credit is entirely spurious and must be removed in full.

### 2.3 Two results

**Proposition 1 (expected discount).** The divergence between the true joint distribution and the predictivist's model is

$$D(p\,\|\,q)=\mathbb{E}_p\left[\log\frac{p(T\mid X,\Theta)}{p(T\mid\Theta)}\right]=I(T;X\mid\Theta).$$

By the chain rule for relative entropy (Cover and Thomas 2006, §2.5),

$$\mathbb{E}_{p}\Big[D\big(p(\cdot\mid X,T)\,\|\,q(\cdot\mid X,T)\big)\Big]=I(T;X\mid\Theta)-D(p_{XT}\,\|\,q_{XT})\ \le\ I(T;X\mid\Theta).$$

Pinsker's inequality and Jensen's inequality then give, for any proposition $A$ about $\Theta$ (in particular "$T$ is true"),

$$\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\,\big|q(A\mid X,T)-p(A\mid X,T)\big|\,\Big]\ \le\ \sqrt{I(T;X\mid\Theta)/2}.$$

So the expected absolute error in the posterior probability of the proposed hypothesis, committed by crediting the proposal as if it were predictive, is bounded by a square-root function of the conditional leakage.

**Proposition 2 (single-case identity).** Define the conditional information density

$$i_\theta(t;x)=\log\frac{p(t\mid x,\theta)}{p(t\mid\theta)}.$$

Then for any $\theta_1,\theta_2$,

$$\log\frac{q(\theta_1\mid x,t)/q(\theta_2\mid x,t)}{p(\theta_1\mid x,t)/p(\theta_2\mid x,t)}=i_{\theta_2}(t;x)-i_{\theta_1}(t;x).$$

The proof is direct: the prior and data factors cancel, and what remains are the two proposal factors. Taking $\theta_1$ to be the state in which $t$ is true, the predictivist overstates the odds of $t$ against a rival $\theta_2$ by exactly the excess of the rival's information density over the proposed hypothesis's own.

The derivations are trivial. The philosophical content lies in identifying the right evidence (the proposal event), the right reference model (the factored model $q$), and the right information (conditional on $\Theta$). One further observation connects these results to the statistical literature. For fixed $\theta$, $q$ is exactly the product distribution $P_{T\mid\theta}\otimes P_{X\mid\theta}$. That product is the reference measure in the Russo–Zou proof, which applies the variational characterisation of relative entropy to the divergence between the joint law of $(T,X)$ and this product. Their theorem therefore says that $|\mathbb{E}_p\phi-\mathbb{E}_q\phi|\le\sigma\sqrt{2D(p\|q)}$ for the fit statistic. Proposition 1 says that the posterior distortion is at most $D(p\|q)$. One divergence governs both the frequentist inflation of the fit and the Bayesian distortion of confirmation: the divergence between how proposals were actually generated and the fiction that they were generated independently of the data, given the world.

### 2.4 A worked example

Let $\Theta\in\{0,1\}$ with uniform prior. Let $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(X=\theta)=0.8$. Suppose the proposer has no independent insight and sees the data through a binary symmetric channel: she observes $S$, which equals $X$ with probability $1-\varepsilon$, and she proposes $T=S$.

The proposer's marginal reliability is $a=P(T=\theta)=0.8(1-\varepsilon)+0.2\varepsilon$. The leakage is

$$I(T;X\mid\Theta)=h(1-a)-h(\varepsilon),$$

where $h$ is binary entropy. Because the choice depends on $\theta$ only through $x$, the correct posterior for $\Theta=1$ given $x=t=1$ is $0.8$. The predictivist multiplies the data's likelihood ratio, $4$, by the proposal's ratio, $a/(1-a)$.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## 3. Why the information must be conditional on the world

The original thesis spoke of $I(E;\text{choice of }H)$ without conditioning. That was a mistake, and correcting it is not cosmetic. Consider a theorist with excellent insight who proposes, before any data, the hypothesis the data will then favour. Here $T$ and $X$ are strongly correlated, because both track $\Theta$. So $I(T;X)>0$, yet this is the paradigm of a successful prediction. Only $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$ vanishes in this case, and only that quantity appears in Proposition 1.

The adaptive-data-analysis bounds already use the conditional quantity, though implicitly. They hold the data-generating distribution fixed, so their $I(T;X)$ is computed under the true law, which is $I(T;X\mid\Theta=\theta^*)$.

The correction also sharpens one of my original examples. I had claimed that pre-data choices informed by correlated pilot data involve some leakage. That is right only if the pilot data $Y$ and the main data $X$ are dependent *given $\Theta$*. Examples are a shared instrument with a systematic offset, overlapping samples, or a common analysis pipeline with a bug. If the pilot study is merely another draw from the same world, then $Y\perp X\mid\Theta$. By the data-processing inequality, $I(T;X\mid\Theta)\le I(Y;X\mid\Theta)=0$, and the subsequent test is a genuine prediction.

This is the verdict we want. A hypothesis suggested by one independent experiment and then confirmed by another is the textbook case of novel success. A hypothesis tuned to pilot data that share an instrument's bias inherits that bias, and its "confirmation" by the main data is partly an echo of that bias. The conditional formulation separates these two cases. Timing cannot, since both choices precede the main data.

## 4. Reply to (iii): what is bounded is confirmation

The referee poses a dilemma. Either the account makes confirmation procedure-relative, which begs the question against the likelihood principle and needs a defence, or it is a thesis about the error rates of procedures, which makes it a refinement of severity.

I take neither horn.

**The likelihood principle is respected.** The likelihood principle says that the evidential import of an observation $o$ for $\theta$ is exhausted by $p(o\mid\theta)$, read as a function of $\theta$ at the actual $o$ (Birnbaum 1962; Berger and Wolpert 1988; Royall 1997). Apply it to the total evidence $o=(x,t)$. The relevant function is $p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta)$ at the actual $x$ and $t$. Nothing here depends on sample spaces, stopping rules, or what the evidence would have been. The second factor is the likelihood of the proposal event. It depends on the proposer only in the way that $p(x\mid\theta)$ depends on the instrument.

What does depend on counterfactual behaviour is the predictivist's factor $p(t\mid\theta)$, which marginalises over datasets that did not occur. But that factor belongs to the *mistaken* model $q$. The account therefore does not make confirmation procedure-relative. It diagnoses procedure-relativity, through the factor $p(t\mid\theta)$, as the source of the predictivist's error whenever $T\not\perp X\mid\Theta$.

**Dawid's result is a theorem of the account.** Dawid (1994) shows that if the prior over hypotheses is fixed in advance and selection depends only on the data, the posterior for the selected parameter needs no adjustment. In my terms, "selection depends only on the data" means $p(t\mid x,\theta)=p(t\mid x)$. That factor then cancels, and the correct posterior is $p(\theta\mid x)$. I agree that nothing needs discounting *relative to $p(\theta\mid x)$*.

But that was never the predictivist's comparison. The predictivist's claim was that a predicted fit earns more than an accommodated one. Dawid's agent gives the proposal no weight at all, in either case. The question predictivism raises is how much of the credit that a proposal *would* earn, were it independent evidence, survives the proposal's dependence on the data. The answer runs from "all of it" ($I=0$) to "none of it" (Dawid's case). The account says where an episode falls on that range and bounds the error of assuming it falls at the predictive end.

Senn's (2008) discussion supports this division. Whether selection is ignorable depends on whether the probability model applies to the selected quantity before or after selection. That is precisely the question of what the joint model of proposal and data is.

**The fixed prior is the crux.** Dawid's ignorability requires a prior over the hypothesis space fixed before the data. Much real accommodation lacks one. The hypothesis is constructed after the data, and the evaluator's prior for it is formed only on encountering it. A prior formed on encountering $t$ is a prior conditional on the proposal. This is the step at which the predictivist factor $p(t\mid\theta)$ silently enters, and where double counting occurs if the proposal was data-driven. This is also what Worrall's (2014) use-novelty and the climate-calibration debate (Steele and Werndl 2013) are tracking.

Steele and Werndl rightly observe that Bayesian calibration with a fixed prior allows data to be used both for calibration and for confirmation without error. On my account that is Dawid's endpoint again. Double counting becomes an error only for an evaluator who also credits the calibrated model's having been proposed.

**Severity.** I accept that the frequentist half of the picture, the Russo–Zou bound, is naturally read as a bound on the optimism of a fit statistic. It is therefore relevant to severity in Mayo's (1996, ch. 8; 2018) sense. Mayo argues that violating use-novelty matters only insofar as it lowers severity, and the bound quantifies one way it can.

The contribution is not a reduction of Bayesian confirmation to severity, nor the reverse. It is the observation that both are controlled by the *same* divergence, $D(p\|q)$, which compares how proposals actually arise with the fiction that they arise independently of the data given the world. This explains a fact that has puzzled commentators: error statisticians and Bayesian predictivists agree on the cases (blind analysis is good, post-hoc subgroup selection is bad, independent replication restores credibility) while disagreeing about foundations. They agree on cases because both are measuring the cost of the independence fiction.

The chain-rule decomposition in Proposition 1 adds something further. The expected posterior distortion equals the leakage *minus* $D(p_{XT}\|q_{XT})$, the part of the leakage that is detectable from the pair $(x,t)$ alone. Fisher's (1936) charge that Mendel's data fit "too well" is an exploitation of exactly that detectable part: a suspiciously good fit is evidence of leakage. What distorts confirmation is the undetectable remainder.

## 5. Reply to (ii): expectation and the single case

The referee is right that an expected-value bound does not, by itself, fix the discount owed to the case in hand. I offer three replies, in increasing order of strength.

**First, the single case has an exact answer.** Proposition 2 gives the realised discount in log-odds as $i_{\theta_2}(t;x)-i_{\theta_1}(t;x)$. Mutual information is the mean of these densities. So the realised discount is an information-theoretic quantity of the same family as the bound, not something the bound fails to reach.

The identity also explains both of the referee's observations. A small average leakage is compatible with a large realised discount when the realised densities are atypically large. A large average leakage is compatible with no discount here when the densities happen to be equal across rivals, that is, when the proposer's choice was, at this dataset, no more probable under one hypothesis than another relative to baseline. The account predicts both phenomena rather than being refuted by them.

**Second, the average does constrain the single case, probabilistically.** The posterior divergence $D(p(\cdot\mid x,t)\,\|\,q(\cdot\mid x,t))$ is non-negative with mean at most $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$. By Markov's inequality, the probability that it exceeds $I/\delta$ is at most $\delta$. So "small average, large realised distortion" is possible only on events whose probability the average itself bounds. This is weak, but it is a genuine single-case guarantee.

**Third, uniform single-case bounds are available, and they are still information bounds.** The referee suggests that moving to max-information (Dwork et al. 2015b; Rogers et al. 2016) abandons mutual information and with it the thesis. I think the right lesson is different. Pointwise information densities, mutual information (their mean), and max-information (their supremum) are three functionals of a single object: the information density between data and choice. The thesis should be stated about that object, and the choice of functional should follow the epistemic question being asked. The expected discount is governed by the mean. A uniform single-case discount is governed by the sup.

Concretely, define two-sided conditional max-information as $M=\sup_{\theta,x,t}|i_\theta(t;x)|$. Proposition 2 then gives a log-odds discount of at most $2M$ in every case. $M$ is bounded whenever the channel from data to proposer is differentially private. If changing one of $n$ observations alters the probability of any proposal by a factor of at most $e^{\varepsilon}$, then by group privacy $p(t\mid x,\theta)/p(t\mid x',\theta)\le e^{n\varepsilon}$ for any two datasets. Since $p(t\mid\theta)$ is a mixture of such terms, $|i_\theta(t;x)|\le n\varepsilon$. Sharper approximate bounds, which hold with probability $1-\beta$, are given by Dwork et al. (2015b) and Rogers et al. (2016).

For the frequentist half, Dwork et al. (2015b) show that if the proposer's view of the data has a description of at most $k$ bits, then the $\beta$-approximate max-information is at most $k+\log_2(1/\beta)$ bits. Consequently, any event (for instance, "the fit exceeds threshold $c$") that would have probability $\pi$ under independence has probability at most $2^k\pi+\beta$ under the actual dependence. That is a single-case, high-probability guarantee for the coarse-histogram and one-variable-among-many examples below.

So the thesis does survive the substitution, once it is stated at the right level of generality. What it predicts is that the right single-case quantity is information-theoretic and reduces to zero exactly for predictions. Both predictions hold.

Finally, consider what an evaluator can usually know. An evaluator who can compute $i_\theta(t;x)$ at the actual pair should use Proposition 2 and is done. An evaluator who knows only the channel, for example "she saw a 10-bin histogram", is not in a position to compute the realised density. For that evaluator, the honest posterior integrates over models of the proposer, and the expected and uniform bounds are exactly the information they possess. Bounds are not second-best confirmation values. They are what confirmation theory can say about an episode described at the grain at which it is actually known.

## 6. Reply to (i): indeterminacy and the reference class

The objection runs as follows. A scientist who looks at the data and proposes $H$ has no well-defined selection rule over other datasets. So $I$ is indeterminate, and my examples get their verdicts only because I stipulate procedures.

**First, the indeterminacy is predictivism's problem, not mine.** The pair $(x,t)$ has the same content whether $t$ was proposed before or after $x$. Any account on which the timing matters must say *why* the timing matters, and the only available answer appeals to how the proposal was generated: what the proposer would have proposed, under various states of the world, given what they knew. White's reliability, Maher's method, Lipton's fudging, and Hitchcock and Sober's overfitting all appeal to this. So if confirmation is a relation between the actual $E$ and the actual $H$ alone, then there is no predictivist premium, and nothing for the prediction/accommodation distinction to conceal. That is the Howson–Urbach position, and on it the referee's objection has nothing to bite on.

If the premium is real, it is real because of facts about generating processes. Then the indeterminacy the referee identifies afflicts the premium itself: one cannot credit a prediction to a proposer's reliability without a model of the proposer. My account inherits this reference-class problem, as all likelihoods do (Hájek 2007). It does not create it.

**Second, the bounds need the channel, not the policy.** Suppose the data reached the proposer only through a summary $S=g(X,U)$, where $U$ is noise independent of everything else, and that the proposal then depends on $S$ together with private information independent of $X$ given $\Theta$. Then $\Theta, X, S, T$ form a Markov chain conditional on $\Theta$. By the data-processing inequality,

$$I(T;X\mid\Theta)\le I(S;X\mid\Theta),$$

and max-information likewise cannot increase under post-processing (Dwork et al. 2015b). The bound therefore holds *uniformly over all policies* mapping $S$ to proposals. The indeterminate part, the proposer's psychology, does not need to be specified.

What must be specified is the channel. That is a fact about the episode's causal history: what plot was on the screen, which variables were unblinded, what offset the blinding software added. It is counterfactual in the same way an instrument's likelihood is counterfactual, since it says what would have been displayed had the data differed. But it is grounded in hardware and software, not in dispositions. My examples are therefore not stipulations. "Blind" is a physical restriction on $S$, and the verdict for blind analysis is robust because it quantifies over every policy the analyst might have had.

**Third, residual uncertainty yields bounds, not undefinedness.** If the evaluator is unsure which channel or policy operated and represents this as a variable $\Pi$, independent of $X$ given $\Theta$, then

$$I(T;X\mid\Theta)\le I(T,\Pi;X\mid\Theta)=I(T;X\mid\Theta,\Pi)=\mathbb{E}_\Pi\big[I_\pi\big].$$

Uncertainty about the procedure is thus absorbed into a bound by the expected leakage across the procedures one considers possible. Since the thesis is stated as a bound, indeterminacy weakens what can be asserted without making it ill-defined.

**Fourth, the worst case still has a policy-free answer.** When the channel is the identity (the scientist saw everything) and the policy is unknown, the leakage bound reduces to $H(T\mid\Theta)$, which depends on the unknown policy. Two policy-free resources remain.

On the frequentist side there is the Occam bound (Blumer et al. 1987). Fix, before the data, any code or prior $m$ over $\mathcal{H}$. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every hypothesis, the gap between in-sample and true fit for a $[0,1]$-bounded loss on $n$ observations is at most

$$\sqrt{\big(\ln(1/m(t))+\ln(1/\delta)\big)/2n}.$$

This holds for any selection rule whatsoever. Its penalty is the self-information of the hypothesis *actually chosen* under the reference measure, which is a feature of the actual $H$, as the referee demands. Since $\mathbb{E}[-\log m(T)]\ge H(T)\ge I(T;X)$, it is the policy-free, single-case member of the same family.

On the Bayesian side, the corresponding resource is Dawid's: an agent with a prior fixed in advance who gives the proposal no weight is immune to leakage. It is notable that the frequentist and Bayesian escape routes share one condition, *a measure over hypotheses fixed before the data*. They also share one interpretation. In the absence of such a measure, it is the proposal that supplies one, and the proposal is exactly what leakage contaminates.

So where the policy is truly indeterminate and the channel unrestricted, the account gives a definite recommendation: take the full discount and give the proposal no weight. This is no embarrassment. It is the conservative default the methodological literature already enforces through pre-registration and the "garden of forking paths" critique (Gelman and Loken 2014). What the account adds is that this is only the endpoint of a scale. Wherever the channel was restricted, less than the full discount is owed, and the restriction tells us how much less.

## 7. The continuum, and what timing tracks

With the channel bounds in hand, the continuum promised in the original sketch can be populated. Each case below warrants intermediate confirmation in the precise sense of Proposition 1. The proposal retains part of its predictive credit, and the error in crediting all of it is bounded by the channel.

- **Noisy summary.** The proposer sees $S=X+N$ with Gaussian noise of variance $\tau^2$, where $X$ has conditional variance $\sigma^2$ per coordinate across $d$ coordinates. Then $I(S;X\mid\Theta)\le\frac{d}{2}\log(1+\sigma^2/\tau^2)$. This approaches zero as the noise grows. Section 2.4 gave the binary version, in which the discount and the bound fall together.
- **Coarse histogram.** The proposer sees bin counts over $k$ bins from $n$ observations. The leakage is at most $\log\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}\le(k-1)\log(n+1)$, and the description-length max-information bound applies with $\log_2$ of the same count.
- **One variable among many.** The proposer screens $m$ candidate variables and proposes a hypothesis about the best-looking one. The selection carries at most $\log m$ of leakage, however the subsequent hypothesis about that variable was formed from prior knowledge. The familiar Bonferroni intuition thus appears here as a statement about the *evidential weight of a proposal*, not only about error rates.
- **Blind analysis.** In particle physics, analysts fix selection criteria on data that have been shifted by a hidden offset, hidden in signal regions, or replaced by simulation (Klein and Roodman 2005). An offset uniform over a compact group makes the blinded view statistically independent of the true value, giving zero leakage after the data are in hand. Practical blinding leaks through control regions and offsets of bounded range, so it lies near zero rather than at it.
- **Shared-bias pilot data.** As in §3, a pre-data choice leaks exactly as much as the pilot data share with the main data beyond what the world explains.

Timing now takes its proper place. "Proposed before the data" is the statement that there is no channel from $X$ to $T$. Unless the proposer's other inputs depend on $X$ given $\Theta$, this guarantees zero leakage. "Proposed after the data" says only that a channel *could* exist, and it supports nothing beyond the trivial bound $H(T\mid\Theta)$.

Timing is therefore a one-bit report on a quantity that is not one-bit. It is neither necessary for zero leakage (blind post-data choice) nor sufficient for it (pre-data choice through a dependent pilot). It is useful for the same reason any crude bound is useful: it is easy to verify. The predictivist tradition was right that something epistemically important is tracked by "use-novelty". It mistook a sufficient condition for the absence of leakage for the thing itself.

The account also fits the cases that have pushed predictivists towards "weak" predictivism (Barnes 2008), on which prediction matters only as a symptom of something else. Hitchcock and Sober (2004) argue that prediction matters as evidence against overfitting, and that accommodation is harmless where overfitting is not a risk. My account identifies the something else, the conditional information flow from data to proposal, and says how much of it there was.

## 8. Limits

Four limits should be stated plainly.

First, the bounds can be loose. In §2.4 the expected discount ran at roughly a third to a half of $\sqrt{I/2}$. For specific well-behaved procedures, sharper analyses exist. For maximum-likelihood fitting of $k$ parameters in regular models, Akaike's (1973) result puts the expected optimism of the maximised log-likelihood at about $k$, and Hitchcock and Sober build on this. Worse, for deterministic continuous fitting $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$ is infinite and the mutual-information bound is vacuous. Quantising reported parameters to precision $\varepsilon$ restores finiteness at roughly $k\log(R/\varepsilon)$, which is still loose. Refinements such as Steinke and Zakynthinou's (2020) conditional mutual information, or the per-sample bounds following Xu and Raginsky (2017), address this. I claim only that *some* functional of the information density controls the discount, and that mutual information is the right one for expected discounts under arbitrary policies over a given channel. For a known regular procedure one should use the procedure-specific result, which will lie within the bound.

Second, the framework assumes that the proposer's independent access $Z$ is independent of $X$ given $\Theta$. When "insight" is itself shaped by the field's familiarity with similar datasets, that assumption fails, and the leakage calculation must include those routes. This is a feature, since it is where historically tuned research programmes acquire unearned credibility. But it makes the channel harder to identify.

Third, Proposition 1 measures the discount against a particular evaluator, the predictivist $q$, who uses the proposer's true marginal reliability. An evaluator who misjudges that reliability makes a different error, which the account does not bound.

Fourth, the thesis concerns the proposal's evidential weight. It does not say that accommodation lowers the evidential import of the *data* for the hypothesis. On this point the likelihoodist and Howson–Urbach are, I think, simply right.

## 9. Conclusion

The referee's objection showed that a frequentist bias bound, glossed directly as a claim about confirmation, does not reach confirmation. The repair is not to abandon the information-theoretic thesis but to locate it correctly. Confirmation is relative to total evidence, and total evidence includes the fact that a hypothesis was proposed. The predictivist premium is the weight of that fact when it is independent of the data given the world. The accommodation discount is the error of crediting that weight when it is not.

The expected error is bounded by $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$. The realised error is a difference of information densities. Both are controlled by the channel through which data reached the proposer, whatever the proposer's dispositions. Dawid's ignorability is the full-discount endpoint, and prediction is the zero-discount endpoint. Timing reports, in one bit, on which side of a channel the proposal fell. The same divergence that inflates a selected hypothesis's apparent fit distorts its apparent confirmation, which is why the frequentist and the Bayesian predictivist, starting from incompatible foundations, have long agreed on the cases.

# Leakage, Not Timing: An Information-Theoretic Account of the Accommodation Discount

## 1. Introduction

Predictivism holds that evidence a hypothesis predicted supports it more than evidence it was built to accommodate. The view has been defended on Bayesian grounds (Maher 1988; Lipton 2004; White 2003; Hitchcock and Sober 2004; Barnes 2008), restricted on error-statistical grounds (Mayo 1996, 2018), and rejected by those who take confirmation to be a timeless relation between evidence and hypothesis (Howson and Urbach 2006). I defend the following thesis. How far a fit's confirmatory force should be discounted for accommodation is controlled by the information that flowed from the data into the choice of hypothesis. "Prediction" is the case where that flow is zero. Timing matters only because it is a coarse indicator of whether any flow occurred.

My motivation came from adaptive data analysis. Russo and Zou (2016, 2020) showed that if a statistic $\phi_t(X)$ is $\sigma$-subgaussian for each fixed $t$, and a hypothesis $T$ is selected using the data $X$, then

$$\big|\mathbb{E}[\phi_T(X)-\mu_T]\big| \le \sigma\sqrt{2\,I(T;X)}.$$

Related results by Dwork et al. (2015a, 2015b, 2015c) bound selection bias by quantities such as max-information and differential privacy. The tempting philosophical gloss is that accommodation inflates apparent support in proportion to information leakage.

A referee raised a three-part objection to this gloss, and I think it is correct as aimed at it. First, $I(T;X)$ is a property of a selection *policy*, which is a counterfactual and often indeterminate thing. Confirmation, by contrast, relates the actual $E$ to the actual $H$. Second, an expected-bias bound cannot bound the discount owed in the single case. Third, the quantity being bounded is a frequentist excess of fit, not confirmation. Dawid (1994) showed that for a Bayesian with a fixed prior, data-dependent selection is ignorable. So the thesis either begs the question against the likelihood principle or collapses into a refinement of severity.

This essay restates the thesis so that it survives these points. The restatement makes four changes.

1. **Relocation.** The discount does not attach to the evidential import of the data. It attaches to the evidential import of a second observation: *that this hypothesis was proposed*. On this reading, the account is ordinary total-evidence Bayesianism and complies with the likelihood principle.
2. **Conditioning.** The relevant information is $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$, leakage *given the world*, not $I(T;X)$. The unconditional quantity would wrongly count a reliable theorist's correct prediction as leakage.
3. **Two levels.** In the single case the discount is given *exactly* by pointwise information densities. Their mean, the mutual information, bounds the expected discount. Their supremum, a two-sided max-information, bounds the single case uniformly.
4. **Channels, not policies.** The bounds depend only on the information channel through which the data reached the proposer, which is fixed by the causal history of the episode. They do not depend on the proposer's indeterminate dispositions.

With these changes the original claim survives. The prediction/accommodation dichotomy conceals a continuum, and the continuum lives in confirmation theory proper, not merely in the theory of error rates. Section 2 sets up the framework and proves two simple results. Section 3 defends the conditioning. Sections 4–6 answer the objection's three parts, in the order (iii), (ii), (i), because the answer to (iii) supplies the machinery for the other two. Section 7 locates timing on the continuum. Section 8 states limits.

## 2. The proposal as evidence

### 2.1 The setup

Let $\Theta$ range over candidate states of the world. For simplicity, identify each state with a hypothesis in a countable space $\mathcal{H}$; nothing turns on this. Let $X$ be the data, and let $T\in\mathcal{H}$ be the hypothesis a scientist puts forward as the one to be assessed. The joint distribution is

$$p(\theta,x,t)=p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta).$$

The factor $p(t\mid x,\theta)$ models the proposer. It can depend on $\theta$ in two ways. One route runs through $x$. The other runs through whatever else the proposer has access to that bears on $\theta$: theoretical insight, background knowledge, analogies, other experiments. Write $Z$ for that other access, and assume for now that it is conditionally independent of $X$ given $\Theta$.

An evaluator who learns that $t$ was proposed and that the data are $x$ has total evidence $(x,t)$. The correct posterior is

$$p(\theta\mid x,t)\ \propto\ p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta).$$

This already contains the key point. The proposal event is an observation with its own likelihood. Whether it is evidentially relevant, and how much, depends on how $p(t\mid x,\theta)$ varies with $\theta$ at the actual $(x,t)$.

### 2.2 Prediction and the predictivist evaluator

Call a proposal *predictive*, in the structural sense, iff $T\perp X\mid \Theta$. In that case $p(t\mid x,\theta)=p(t\mid\theta)$ and the likelihood factors:

$$p(\theta\mid x,t)\ \propto\ p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid\theta).$$

The proposal now contributes the ratio $p(t\mid\theta)/p(t\mid\theta')$. This is the proposer's reliability: how much more often this proposer would put $t$ forward if $\theta$ held than if $\theta'$ did. It is the quantity that the Bayesian defences of predictivism exploit. White (2003) argues that a successful prediction is evidence that the theorist was reliably tracking the truth. Maher (1988) argues that it is evidence about the method that produced the hypothesis. Lipton (2004) argues that accommodation raises the suspicion of a "fudged" theory. In each case, the premium for prediction is the evidential weight of the proposal.

Now define the **predictivist evaluator** $q$. This evaluator applies the factored likelihood whatever the proposal's actual provenance:

$$q(\theta,x,t)=p(\theta)\,p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid\theta),$$

where $p(t\mid\theta)=\sum_x p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta)$ is the proposer's true marginal reliability. This evaluator does the natural thing with a track record. They know how often this proposer's hypotheses are true, they see that the data fit, and they multiply. For predictions, $q=p$ and the computation is exact.

I define the **accommodation discount** as the difference between the $q$-posterior and the $p$-posterior. It is the excess apparent support that a hypothesis receives when its proposal is credited as independent evidence even though it was not independent of the data. This is the explicandum of the thesis.

One consequence is worth stating immediately. If the proposer's choice depends on $\theta$ *only* through $x$, so that $p(t\mid x,\theta)=p(t\mid x)$, then that factor is constant in $\theta$ and cancels. The correct posterior is just $p(\theta\mid x)$, and the proposal adds nothing. This is Dawid's (1994) ignorability result, seen from inside the framework. Section 4 returns to it. Here I note only that Dawid's case is not a counterexample to the discount. It is the case of *maximal* discount: the predictivist credit is entirely spurious and must be removed in full.

### 2.3 Two results

**Proposition 1 (expected discount).** The divergence between the true joint distribution and the predictivist's model is

$$D(p\,\|\,q)=\mathbb{E}_p\left[\log\frac{p(T\mid X,\Theta)}{p(T\mid\Theta)}\right]=I(T;X\mid\Theta).$$

By the chain rule for relative entropy (Cover and Thomas 2006, §2.5),

$$\mathbb{E}_{p}\Big[D\big(p(\cdot\mid X,T)\,\|\,q(\cdot\mid X,T)\big)\Big]=I(T;X\mid\Theta)-D(p_{XT}\,\|\,q_{XT})\ \le\ I(T;X\mid\Theta).$$

Pinsker's inequality and Jensen's inequality then give, for any proposition $A$ about $\Theta$ (in particular "$T$ is true"),

$$\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\,\big|q(A\mid X,T)-p(A\mid X,T)\big|\,\Big]\ \le\ \sqrt{I(T;X\mid\Theta)/2}.$$

So the expected absolute error in the posterior probability of the proposed hypothesis, committed by crediting the proposal as if it were predictive, is bounded by a square-root function of the conditional leakage.

**Proposition 2 (single-case identity).** Define the conditional information density

$$i_\theta(t;x)=\log\frac{p(t\mid x,\theta)}{p(t\mid\theta)}.$$

Then for any $\theta_1,\theta_2$,

$$\log\frac{q(\theta_1\mid x,t)/q(\theta_2\mid x,t)}{p(\theta_1\mid x,t)/p(\theta_2\mid x,t)}=i_{\theta_2}(t;x)-i_{\theta_1}(t;x).$$

The proof is direct: the prior and data factors cancel, and what remains are the two proposal factors. Taking $\theta_1$ to be the state in which $t$ is true, the predictivist overstates the odds of $t$ against a rival $\theta_2$ by exactly the excess of the rival's information density over the proposed hypothesis's own.

The derivations are trivial. The philosophical content lies in identifying the right evidence (the proposal event), the right reference model (the factored model $q$), and the right information (conditional on $\Theta$). One further observation connects these results to the statistical literature. For fixed $\theta$, $q$ is exactly the product distribution $P_{T\mid\theta}\otimes P_{X\mid\theta}$. That product is the reference measure in the Russo–Zou proof, which applies the variational characterisation of relative entropy to the divergence between the joint law of $(T,X)$ and this product. Their theorem therefore says that $|\mathbb{E}_p\phi-\mathbb{E}_q\phi|\le\sigma\sqrt{2D(p\|q)}$ for the fit statistic. Proposition 1 says that the posterior distortion is at most $D(p\|q)$. One divergence governs both the frequentist inflation of the fit and the Bayesian distortion of confirmation: the divergence between how proposals were actually generated and the fiction that they were generated independently of the data, given the world.

### 2.4 A worked example

Let $\Theta\in\{0,1\}$ with uniform prior. Let $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(X=\theta)=0.8$. Suppose the proposer has no independent insight and sees the data through a binary symmetric channel: she observes $S$, which equals $X$ with probability $1-\varepsilon$, and she proposes $T=S$.

The proposer's marginal reliability is $a=P(T=\theta)=0.8(1-\varepsilon)+0.2\varepsilon$. The leakage is

$$I(T;X\mid\Theta)=h(1-a)-h(\varepsilon),$$

where $h$ is binary entropy. Because the choice depends on $\theta$ only through $x$, the correct posterior for $\Theta=1$ given $x=t=1$ is $0.8$. The predictivist multiplies the data's likelihood ratio, $4$, by the proposal's ratio, $a/(1-a)$.

| $\varepsilon$ | $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$ (nats) | $q(\Theta{=}1\mid 1,1)$ | discount at $(1,1)$ | expected discount | bound $\sqrt{I/2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.500 | 0.941 | 0.141 | 0.141 | 0.500 |
| 0.1 | 0.248 | 0.919 | 0.119 | 0.129 | 0.352 |
| 0.2 | 0.127 | 0.895 | 0.095 | 0.105 | 0.252 |
| 0.3 | 0.053 | 0.867 | 0.067 | 0.074 | 0.163 |
| 0.5 | 0 | 0.800 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

The expected discount averages $|q-p|$ over all outcomes, including those where the proposal disagrees with the data; there the predictivist *understates* support. The discount falls smoothly as leakage falls and vanishes at zero leakage, which is the point where a "post-data" proposal is in effect a coin toss and therefore predictive. At $\varepsilon=0$ the single-case identity gives a log-odds discount of $\log(0.8/0.2)=\log 4$. This is precisely the proposal's apparent likelihood ratio, all of it spurious.

Now let the proposer mix: with probability $\alpha$ she proposes on the basis of insight $Z$, and otherwise she proposes from the data. Mutual information is convex in the channel for a fixed input distribution, and the insight channel contributes zero leakage given $\Theta$. Hence $I(T;X\mid\Theta)\le(1-\alpha)\,I_{\text{fit}}$. In this mixed case, the correct posterior retains part of the proposal's credit.

## 3. Why the information must be conditional on the world

The original thesis spoke of $I(E;\text{choice of }H)$ without conditioning. That was a mistake, and correcting it is not cosmetic. Consider a theorist with excellent insight who proposes, before any data, the hypothesis the data will then favour. Here $T$ and $X$ are strongly correlated, because both track $\Theta$. So $I(T;X)>0$, yet this is the paradigm of a successful prediction. Only $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$ vanishes in this case, and only that quantity appears in Proposition 1.

The adaptive-data-analysis bounds already use the conditional quantity, though implicitly. They hold the data-generating distribution fixed, so their $I(T;X)$ is computed under the true law, which is $I(T;X\mid\Theta=\theta^*)$.

The correction also sharpens one of my original examples. I had claimed that pre-data choices informed by correlated pilot data involve some leakage. That is right only if the pilot data $Y$ and the main data $X$ are dependent *given $\Theta$*. Examples are a shared instrument with a systematic offset, overlapping samples, or a common analysis pipeline with a bug. If the pilot study is merely another draw from the same world, then $Y\perp X\mid\Theta$. By the data-processing inequality, $I(T;X\mid\Theta)\le I(Y;X\mid\Theta)=0$, and the subsequent test is a genuine prediction.

This is the verdict we want. A hypothesis suggested by one independent experiment and then confirmed by another is the textbook case of novel success. A hypothesis tuned to pilot data that share an instrument's bias inherits that bias, and its "confirmation" by the main data is partly an echo of that bias. The conditional formulation separates these two cases. Timing cannot, since both choices precede the main data.

## 4. Reply to (iii): what is bounded is confirmation

The referee poses a dilemma. Either the account makes confirmation procedure-relative, which begs the question against the likelihood principle and needs a defence, or it is a thesis about the error rates of procedures, which makes it a refinement of severity.

I take neither horn.

**The likelihood principle is respected.** The likelihood principle says that the evidential import of an observation $o$ for $\theta$ is exhausted by $p(o\mid\theta)$, read as a function of $\theta$ at the actual $o$ (Birnbaum 1962; Berger and Wolpert 1988; Royall 1997). Apply it to the total evidence $o=(x,t)$. The relevant function is $p(x\mid\theta)\,p(t\mid x,\theta)$ at the actual $x$ and $t$. Nothing here depends on sample spaces, stopping rules, or what the evidence would have been. The second factor is the likelihood of the proposal event. It depends on the proposer only in the way that $p(x\mid\theta)$ depends on the instrument.

What does depend on counterfactual behaviour is the predictivist's factor $p(t\mid\theta)$, which marginalises over datasets that did not occur. But that factor belongs to the *mistaken* model $q$. The account therefore does not make confirmation procedure-relative. It diagnoses procedure-relativity, through the factor $p(t\mid\theta)$, as the source of the predictivist's error whenever $T\not\perp X\mid\Theta$.

**Dawid's result is a theorem of the account.** Dawid (1994) shows that if the prior over hypotheses is fixed in advance and selection depends only on the data, the posterior for the selected parameter needs no adjustment. In my terms, "selection depends only on the data" means $p(t\mid x,\theta)=p(t\mid x)$. That factor then cancels, and the correct posterior is $p(\theta\mid x)$. I agree that nothing needs discounting *relative to $p(\theta\mid x)$*.

But that was never the predictivist's comparison. The predictivist's claim was that a predicted fit earns more than an accommodated one. Dawid's agent gives the proposal no weight at all, in either case. The question predictivism raises is how much of the credit that a proposal *would* earn, were it independent evidence, survives the proposal's dependence on the data. The answer runs from "all of it" ($I=0$) to "none of it" (Dawid's case). The account says where an episode falls on that range and bounds the error of assuming it falls at the predictive end.

**The fixed prior is the crux.** Dawid's ignorability requires a prior over the hypothesis space fixed before the data. Much real accommodation lacks one. The hypothesis is constructed after the data, and the evaluator's prior for it is formed only on encountering it. A prior formed on encountering $t$ is a prior conditional on the proposal. This is the step at which the predictivist factor $p(t\mid\theta)$ silently enters, and where double counting occurs if the proposal was data-driven. This is also what Worrall's (2014) use-novelty and the climate-calibration debate (Steele and Werndl 2013) are tracking.

Steele and Werndl rightly observe that Bayesian calibration with a fixed prior allows data to be used both for calibration and for confirmation without error. On my account that is Dawid's endpoint again. Double counting becomes an error only for an evaluator who also credits the calibrated model's having been proposed.

**Severity.** I accept that the frequentist half of the picture, the Russo–Zou bound, is naturally read as a bound on the optimism of a fit statistic. It is therefore relevant to severity in Mayo's (1996, ch. 8; 2018) sense. Mayo argues that violating use-novelty matters only insofar as it lowers severity, and the bound quantifies one way it can.

The contribution is not a reduction of Bayesian confirmation to severity, nor the reverse. It is the observation that both are controlled by the *same* divergence, $D(p\|q)$, which compares how proposals actually arise with the fiction that they arise independently of the data given the world. This explains a fact that has puzzled commentators: error statisticians and Bayesian predictivists agree on the cases (blind analysis is good, post-hoc subgroup selection is bad, independent replication restores credibility) while disagreeing about foundations. They agree on cases because both are measuring the cost of the independence fiction.

The chain-rule decomposition in Proposition 1 adds something further, because it splits leakage exactly into two parts. One part, $D(p_{XT}\|q_{XT})$, is the predictivist model's error about the observables: how far the actual distribution of data–proposal pairs departs from what the independence fiction predicts. This part is statistically detectable, though not usually from a single pair. Fisher's (1936) charge that Mendel's data fit "too well" exploits it, since a fit improbable under independence is evidence of leakage. The other part is the expected posterior distortion itself. So all leakage costs the predictivist something, but in two currencies: misprediction of what will be observed, and misjudgement of the world given what was observed. Only the second is a confirmational error. For fixed leakage, it is largest when accommodation is statistically indistinguishable from prediction. The bound of Proposition 1 is accordingly conservative whenever leakage leaves traces in the observables.

## 5. Reply to (ii): expectation and the single case

The referee is right that an expected-value bound does not, by itself, fix the discount owed to the case in hand. I offer three replies, in increasing order of strength.

**First, the single case has an exact answer.** Proposition 2 gives the realised discount in log-odds as $i_{\theta_2}(t;x)-i_{\theta_1}(t;x)$. Mutual information is the mean of these densities. So the realised discount is an information-theoretic quantity of the same family as the bound, not something the bound fails to reach.

The identity also explains both of the referee's observations. A small average leakage is compatible with a large realised discount when the realised densities are atypically large. A large average leakage is compatible with no discount here when the densities happen to be equal across rivals, that is, when the proposer's choice was, at this dataset, no more probable under one hypothesis than another relative to baseline. The account predicts both phenomena rather than being refuted by them.

**Second, the average does constrain the single case, probabilistically.** The posterior divergence $D(p(\cdot\mid x,t)\,\|\,q(\cdot\mid x,t))$ is non-negative with mean at most $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$. By Markov's inequality, the probability that it exceeds $I/\delta$ is at most $\delta$. So "small average, large realised distortion" is possible only on events whose probability the average itself bounds. This is weak, but it is a genuine single-case guarantee.

**Third, uniform single-case bounds are available, and they are still information bounds.** The referee suggests that moving to max-information (Dwork et al. 2015b; Rogers et al. 2016) abandons mutual information and with it the thesis. I think the right lesson is different. Pointwise information densities, mutual information (their mean), and max-information (their supremum) are three functionals of a single object: the information density between data and choice. The thesis should be stated about that object, and the choice of functional should follow the epistemic question being asked. The expected discount is governed by the mean. A uniform single-case discount is governed by the sup.

Concretely, define two-sided conditional max-information as $M=\sup_{\theta,x,t}|i_\theta(t;x)|$. Proposition 2 then gives a log-odds discount of at most $2M$ in every case. $M$ is bounded whenever the channel from data to proposer is differentially private. If changing one of $n$ observations alters the probability of any proposal by a factor of at most $e^{\varepsilon}$, then by group privacy $p(t\mid x,\theta)/p(t\mid x',\theta)\le e^{n\varepsilon}$ for any two datasets. Since $p(t\mid\theta)$ is a mixture of such terms, $|i_\theta(t;x)|\le n\varepsilon$. Sharper approximate bounds, which hold with probability $1-\beta$, are given by Dwork et al. (2015b) and Rogers et al. (2016).

For the frequentist half, Dwork et al. (2015b) show that if the proposer's view of the data has a description of at most $k$ bits, then the $\beta$-approximate max-information is at most $k+\log_2(1/\beta)$ bits. Consequently, any event (for instance, "the fit exceeds threshold $c$") that would have probability $\pi$ under independence has probability at most $2^k\pi+\beta$ under the actual dependence. That is a single-case, high-probability guarantee for the coarse-histogram and one-variable-among-many examples below.

So the thesis does survive the substitution, once it is stated at the right level of generality. What it predicts is that the right single-case quantity is information-theoretic and reduces to zero exactly for predictions. Both predictions hold.

Finally, consider what an evaluator can usually know. An evaluator who can compute $i_\theta(t;x)$ at the actual pair should use Proposition 2 and is done. An evaluator who knows only the channel, for example "she saw a 10-bin histogram", is not in a position to compute the realised density. For that evaluator, the honest posterior integrates over models of the proposer, and the expected and uniform bounds are exactly the information they possess. Bounds are not second-best confirmation values. They are what confirmation theory can say about an episode described at the grain at which it is actually known.

## 6. Reply to (i): indeterminacy and the reference class

The objection runs as follows. A scientist who looks at the data and proposes $H$ has no well-defined selection rule over other datasets. So $I$ is indeterminate, and my examples get their verdicts only because I stipulate procedures.

**First, the indeterminacy is predictivism's problem, not mine.** The pair $(x,t)$ has the same content whether $t$ was proposed before or after $x$. Any account on which the timing matters must say *why* the timing matters, and the only available answer appeals to how the proposal was generated: what the proposer would have proposed, under various states of the world, given what they knew. White's reliability, Maher's method, Lipton's fudging, and Hitchcock and Sober's overfitting all appeal to this. So if confirmation is a relation between the actual $E$ and the actual $H$ alone, then there is no predictivist premium, and nothing for the prediction/accommodation distinction to conceal. That is the Howson–Urbach position, and on it the referee's objection has nothing to bite on.

If the premium is real, it is real because of facts about generating processes. Then the indeterminacy the referee identifies afflicts the premium itself: one cannot credit a prediction to a proposer's reliability without a model of the proposer. My account inherits this reference-class problem, as all likelihoods do (Hájek 2007). It does not create it.

**Second, the bounds need the channel, not the policy.** Suppose the data reached the proposer only through a summary $S=g(X,U)$, where $U$ is noise independent of everything else, and that the proposal then depends on $S$ together with private information independent of $X$ given $\Theta$. Then $\Theta, X, S, T$ form a Markov chain conditional on $\Theta$. By the data-processing inequality,

$$I(T;X\mid\Theta)\le I(S;X\mid\Theta),$$

and max-information likewise cannot increase under post-processing (Dwork et al. 2015b). The bound therefore holds *uniformly over all policies* mapping $S$ to proposals. The indeterminate part, the proposer's psychology, does not need to be specified.

What must be specified is the channel. That is a fact about the episode's causal history: what plot was on the screen, which variables were unblinded, what offset the blinding software added. It is counterfactual in the same way an instrument's likelihood is counterfactual, since it says what would have been displayed had the data differed. But it is grounded in hardware and software, not in dispositions. My examples are therefore not stipulations. "Blind" is a physical restriction on $S$, and the verdict for blind analysis is robust because it quantifies over every policy the analyst might have had.

**Third, residual uncertainty yields bounds, not undefinedness.** If the evaluator is unsure which channel or policy operated and represents this as a variable $\Pi$, independent of $X$ given $\Theta$, then

$$I(T;X\mid\Theta)\le I(T,\Pi;X\mid\Theta)=I(T;X\mid\Theta,\Pi)=\mathbb{E}_\Pi\big[I_\pi\big].$$

Uncertainty about the procedure is thus absorbed into a bound by the expected leakage across the procedures one considers possible. Since the thesis is stated as a bound, indeterminacy weakens what can be asserted without making it ill-defined.

**Fourth, the worst case still has a policy-free answer.** When the channel is the identity (the scientist saw everything) and the policy is unknown, the leakage bound reduces to $H(T\mid\Theta)$, which depends on the unknown policy. Two policy-free resources remain.

On the frequentist side there is the Occam bound (Blumer et al. 1987). Fix, before the data, any code or prior $m$ over $\mathcal{H}$. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every hypothesis, the gap between in-sample and true fit for a $[0,1]$-bounded loss on $n$ observations is at most

$$\sqrt{\big(\ln(1/m(t))+\ln(1/\delta)\big)/2n}.$$

This holds for any selection rule whatsoever. Its penalty is the self-information of the hypothesis *actually chosen* under the reference measure, which is a feature of the actual $H$, as the referee demands. Since $\mathbb{E}[-\log m(T)]\ge H(T)\ge I(T;X)$, it is the policy-free, single-case member of the same family.

On the Bayesian side, the corresponding resource is Dawid's: an agent with a prior fixed in advance who gives the proposal no weight is immune to leakage. It is notable that the frequentist and Bayesian escape routes share one condition, *a measure over hypotheses fixed before the data*. They also share one interpretation. In the absence of such a measure, it is the proposal that supplies one, and the proposal is exactly what leakage contaminates.

So where the policy is truly indeterminate and the channel unrestricted, the account gives a definite recommendation: take the full discount and give the proposal no weight. This is no embarrassment. It is the conservative default the methodological literature already enforces through pre-registration and the "garden of forking paths" critique (Gelman and Loken 2014). What the account adds is that this is only the endpoint of a scale. Wherever the channel was restricted, less than the full discount is owed, and the restriction tells us how much less.

## 7. The continuum, and what timing tracks

With the channel bounds in hand, the continuum promised in the original sketch can be populated. Each case below warrants intermediate confirmation in the precise sense of Proposition 1. The proposal retains part of its predictive credit, and the error in crediting all of it is bounded by the channel.

- **Noisy summary.** The proposer sees $S=X+N$ with Gaussian noise of variance $\tau^2$, where $X$ has conditional variance $\sigma^2$ per coordinate across $d$ coordinates. Then $I(S;X\mid\Theta)\le\frac{d}{2}\log(1+\sigma^2/\tau^2)$. This approaches zero as the noise grows.
- **Coarse histogram.** The proposer sees bin counts over $k$ bins from $n$ observations. The leakage is at most $\log\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}\le(k-1)\log(n+1)$, and the description-length max-information bound applies with $\log_2$ of the same count.
- **One variable among many.** The proposer screens $m$ candidate variables and proposes a hypothesis about the best-looking one. The selection carries at most $\log m$ of leakage, however the subsequent hypothesis about that variable was formed from prior knowledge. The familiar Bonferroni intuition thus appears here as a statement about the *evidential weight of a proposal*, not only about error rates.
- **Blind analysis.** In particle physics, analysts fix selection criteria on data that have been shifted by a hidden offset, hidden in signal regions, or replaced by simulation (Klein and Roodman 2005). An offset uniform over a compact group makes the blinded view statistically independent of the true value, giving zero leakage after the data are in hand. Practical blinding leaks through control regions and offsets of bounded range, so it lies near zero rather than at it.
- **Shared-bias pilot data.** As in §3, a pre-data choice leaks exactly as much as the pilot data share with the main data beyond what the world explains.

Timing now takes its proper place. "Proposed before the data" is the statement that there is no channel from $X$ to $T$. Unless the proposer's other inputs depend on $X$ given $\Theta$, this guarantees zero leakage. "Proposed after the data" says only that a channel *could* exist, and it supports nothing beyond the trivial bound $H(T\mid\Theta)$.

Timing is therefore a one-bit report on a quantity that is not one-bit. It is neither necessary for zero leakage (blind post-data choice) nor sufficient for it (pre-data choice through a dependent pilot). It is useful for the same reason any crude bound is useful: it is easy to verify. The predictivist tradition was right that something epistemically important is tracked by "use-novelty". It mistook a sufficient condition for the absence of leakage for the thing itself.

The account also fits the cases that have pushed predictivists towards "weak" predictivism (Barnes 2008), on which prediction matters only as a symptom of something else. Hitchcock and Sober (2004) argue that prediction matters as evidence against overfitting, and that accommodation is harmless where overfitting is not a risk. My account identifies the something else, the conditional information flow from data to proposal, and says how much of it there was.

## 8. Limits

Four limits should be stated plainly.

First, the bounds can be loose. In §2.4 the expected discount ran at roughly a third to a half of $\sqrt{I/2}$. For specific well-behaved procedures, sharper analyses exist. For maximum-likelihood fitting of $k$ parameters in regular models, Akaike's (1973) result puts the expected optimism of the maximised log-likelihood at about $k$, and Hitchcock and Sober build on this. Worse, for deterministic continuous fitting $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$ is infinite and the mutual-information bound is vacuous. Quantising reported parameters to precision $\varepsilon$ restores finiteness at roughly $k\log(R/\varepsilon)$, which is still loose. Refinements such as Steinke and Zakynthinou's (2020) conditional mutual information, or the per-sample bounds following Xu and Raginsky (2017), address this. I claim only that *some* functional of the information density controls the discount, and that mutual information is the right one for expected discounts under arbitrary policies over a given channel. For a known regular procedure one should use the procedure-specific result, which will lie within the bound.

Second, the framework assumes that the proposer's independent access $Z$ is independent of $X$ given $\Theta$. When "insight" is itself shaped by the field's familiarity with similar datasets, that assumption fails, and the leakage calculation must include those routes. This is a feature, since it is where historically tuned research programmes acquire unearned credibility. But it makes the channel harder to identify.

Third, Proposition 1 measures the discount against a particular evaluator, the predictivist $q$, who uses the proposer's true marginal reliability. An evaluator who misjudges that reliability makes a different error, which the account does not bound.

Fourth, the thesis concerns the proposal's evidential weight. It does not say that accommodation lowers the evidential import of the *data* for the hypothesis. On this point the likelihoodist and Howson–Urbach are, I think, simply right.

## 9. Conclusion

The referee's objection showed that a frequentist bias bound, glossed directly as a claim about confirmation, does not reach confirmation. The repair is not to abandon the information-theoretic thesis but to locate it correctly. Confirmation is relative to total evidence, and total evidence includes the fact that a hypothesis was proposed. The predictivist premium is the weight of that fact when it is independent of the data given the world. The accommodation discount is the error of crediting that weight when it is not.

The expected error is bounded by $I(T;X\mid\Theta)$. The realised error is a difference of information densities. Both are controlled by the channel through which data reached the proposer, whatever the proposer's dispositions. Dawid's ignorability is the full-discount endpoint, and prediction is the zero-discount endpoint. Timing reports, in one bit, on which side of a channel the proposal fell. The same divergence that inflates a selected hypothesis's apparent fit distorts its apparent confirmation, which is why the frequentist and the Bayesian predictivist, starting from incompatible foundations, have long agreed on the cases.
